text: In information theory, what does a low perplexity indicate?
options: The model is good at predicting the sample
The model has few parameters to train
The training data was collected recently
The model runs slowly at inference time
answer: The model is good at predicting the sample
explanation: It measures how well a probability distribution predicts a sample, and lower means better. The intuitive version is that perplexity is roughly how many options the model feels it has at each step, so 2 means it is usually confident between two choices.

text: A model is overfitting when it does what?
options: Has too few parameters to learn the pattern
Fits the training data too closely to generalise
Runs out of memory during training
Produces the same output for every input
answer: Fits the training data too closely to generalise
explanation: It corresponds too closely to one particular set of data and then fails on anything new, and an overfitted model has more parameters than the data can justify. Every regularisation technique, dropout included, exists to stop this, and large language models are trained in a regime where it is deliberately taken to the extreme.

text: Gradient descent is what kind of method?
options: A stochastic sampling algorithm
A method for compressing model weights
An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
A procedure for splitting a dataset into batches
answer: An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
explanation: A first order iterative algorithm for minimising a differentiable function, which means it follows the slope downhill in small steps. The batch size and learning rate are the two hyperparameters everyone tunes first, and the reason the loss curve is noisy rather than smooth is that each step uses a different sample of the data.

text: Dropout is a technique for reducing what problem in neural networks?
options: Vanishing gradients
Class imbalance
Slow convergence
Overfitting
explanation: Overfitting, by randomly zeroing inputs and outputs during training so neurons cannot co-adapt to each other. It is only applied while training and never at inference, which is the detail that trips people up when they first see it in code.

options: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
The next token in the output sequence
The attention weights between two tokens
The size of the model's parameter count
answer: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
explanation: Gradient computation for the parameter updates, by working backwards through the network and applying the chain rule. It is the reason training is not guesswork, and the reason the transformer abandoned backpropagation through time, since the whole sequence is processed in one forward pass instead.

text: A latent space is best described as what?
options: A physical region where models are stored on disk
A space where similar items sit close together
A list of tokens the model has never seen
The gap between training and inference
answer: A space where similar items sit close together
explanation: An embedding space defined by a set of latent variables that emerge from how similar items resemble each other. The geometry is the point, because it is what makes nearest neighbour search, clustering and the whole idea of interpolating between two images work.

text: Zero-shot learning is a setup where the learner sees what during training?
options: Only unlabelled images of the target classes
One labelled example of every class
No examples at all of the test time classes
Labels provided only at test time
answer: No examples at all of the test time classes
explanation: Nothing of the kind, and at test time it has to predict a class it has never seen, which is the name. It is a play on one-shot learning from computer vision, and it is the mechanism behind a large share of what people call a language model doing a task nobody trained it on.

text: What does the ReLU activation function do?
options: Squashes its input between zero and one
Halves its input when it is negative
Converts its input to a probability
Outputs the non negative part of its input
answer: Outputs the non negative part of its input
explanation: It is the ramp function, zero below zero and linear above, and being non linear is what lets a network of them solve non trivial problems. It replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers because it does not saturate on the positive side and it is far cheaper to compute.

text: What does the softmax function convert a tuple of numbers into?
options: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
A single averaged value
A sorted list in descending order
A gradient for each input weight
answer: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
explanation: A probability distribution over K outcomes, and it is almost always the last activation function in a classifier or language model. It is a generalisation of the logistic function to multiple dimensions, which is why you see the same function doing both binary and 50,000 way classification.

text: What is an epoch in neural network training?
options: One batch of data processed by the model
One full pass through the entire training dataset
One full pass of the loss function over the weights
One forward pass through a single layer
answer: One full pass through the entire training dataset
explanation: A full pass over the training data, after which the batch count resets. People say one epoch on a frontier model almost in the abstract, because the dataset is so large that nobody sees a second one, which is a good way to notice that the word is doing less work than people assume.
